verdicts.trueWording: the necessity of assembling the meaning of the text from numerous seemingly disconnected clues
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200, browser UA). Byline 'By Nick Gevers', dated 5 September 2000 (2000-09-05T19:32:56 in the markup), title 'The Reader as Augur'. Quote appears word for word in the Calde section. Page's exact framing: 'Quetzal's remarks offer rich insight ... and state volume three's operating instructions to the reader: the necessity of assembling the meaning of the text from numerous seemingly disconnected clues, the need to trust the narrator no further than necessary'. The instructions are attributed to volume three, so the claim's 'volume three states as its terms of reading' holds; the vehicle is Quetzal's remarks.

verdicts.trueWording: The augural eye can perceive the 'hastily erected' 'triumphal arch' (p. 379) as a sign of the generally makeshift nature of the revolutionary regime of which Silk is now calde
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the Calde Epilogue section. Both physical details ('hastily erected', 'triumphal arch', p. 379) and the makeshift-regime reading are on the page; 'new' regime is supported by 'the revolutionary regime of which Silk is now calde' following the uprising.

verdicts.trueWording: After Horn has identified himself as the narrator of Long Sun in the section entitled 'My Defense' (pp. 370-382), thus forcing the reader to re-appraise the whole of the preceding text
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the Exodus section. Nuance recorded, not a defect: 'My Defense' (pp. 370-382) is followed by a separate two-page 'Afterward' (pp. 382-383) by an unnamed narrator, so the self-identification sits in the concluding section of Horn's narrative rather than the literal final pages; the page frames the whole passage as how 'Exodus concludes'.

verdicts.trueWording: The novel's somewhat famous opening sentence reads
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Blog 'Strange at Ecbatan', author Rich Horton, post dated August 18, 2024 - consistent with the cited 'August 2024'. Quote verbatim, immediately preceding the quoted elm-tree sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: We learn later that Eleanor Bold planted trees on the graves of her friends ... One assumes, then, that the elm tree that has just fallen was planted on Weer's grave
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Every limb on the page: the legend is supplied later ('We learn later'; 'there is an old legend that when a tree planted on one's grave falls, the ghost ... is released'), and the inference is Horton's own ('One assumes, then').

verdicts.trueWording: which tells us too that this narration is likely decades if not more after Weer's death
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, in the same sentence as the grave inference, so 'from that same detail' is supported by 'which tells us too'.

verdicts.trueWording: There are also a great many lacunae. Very few of the stories actually come to an end
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; 'lacunae' is italicised in the markup (lacunae.), which is why a naive tag-strip inserts a space - the rendered sentence is exactly 'There are also a great many lacunae.' The second limb is the immediately following sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: One sentence, guys. Some of them are a struggle to get through but the effort is so worth it!
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200); post dated 2016-08-20 on Tree Slices. The remark follows two full block quotations of long Peace sentences from p. 15, the second introduced as 'Or this sentence, further down the same page' - so both limbs (quoting a Peace sentence in full; remarking it is a single sentence) are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: only in novels does the voice of the narrator construct it, revealing some truths and concealing others
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Byline Andy Lee, Lit & Chess, dated 2026-07-12 in the markup ('Jul 12, 2026'). Quote verbatim; the antecedent of 'it' is 'the world' from the preceding clause about film and television, supporting 'constructs the world of a novel'.

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe never shows you the monster directly
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, in the paragraph beginning 'What raises Peace from a good mystery yarn', exactly as the claim's page hint states.

verdicts.trueWording: These narrative tricks are akin to Poe's 'The Purloined Letter,' the hiding of answers in plain sight
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the same paragraph. The 'narrative tricks' referent includes Wolfe's method in Peace ('Wolfe never shows you the monster directly ... He leaves breadcrumbs'), alongside Wallace and Nabokov, so the likening limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: It could be the story of a conventional life, but the gaps are troubling
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the paragraph on Weer's formative years, preceded by 'There are gaps along the way as Weer grows up'.

verdicts.trueWording: Weer, it seems, is searching for something in his memories, but he's also trying to conceal a whole lot more
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim (curly apostrophe matches), the sentence closing the same paragraph.

verdicts.trueWording: but nevertheless it is catalogued, there it is on the page, a part of the collective history
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Every limb on the page: Louis Gold is introduced as 'a seller of rare but counterfeit books'; the volume is one he has just forged ('This book on my lap - I just wrote it'; 'I thought you just wrote it.' / 'Nevertheless it is catalogued.'); and Lee glosses the line as running from fabricated to catalogued to 'a part of the collective history', which is the claim's 'a record confers existence on what it lists'. Lee's own headline phrase is 'captures the power of narrative beautifully' - a narrative rather than archival emphasis, but the cataloguing-confers-existence reading is explicit in his gloss.

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe's own comments about Peace suggest that he was concerned that he'd done too good of a job, that readers weren't getting it
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Both limbs supported: the comments are Wolfe's own, relayed unspecified by Lee, and the worry is that the concealment worked too well for readers ('that readers weren't getting it').
